M edications are commonly given orally to cats in the form of capsules or tablets. Abnormal esophageal transit of tablets and capsules is a well-recognized phenomenon in humans, and prolonged transit times and entrapment have been reported. 1-4 Delayed esophageal transit is considered problematic, because entrapped tablets and capsules disintegrate within the esophagus, resulting in prolonged exposure of the mucosa to a high concentration of a medication. 5-9 Many medications have been shown to be ulcerogenic, and retention of tablets and capsules is thought to be a common mechanism of esophageal injury in humans. 6 Little attention has been paid to esophageal transit of tablets and capsules in domestic animals. A recent report describes a cat with a small radio-opaque esophageal foreign body that was subsequently ascertained to be an antibiotic tablet given some time before the radiographic examination. 10 In

theory, cats and dogs may be at greater risk of esophageal retention of tablets or capsules than humans, because, unlike humans, they do not have an upright posture, so swallowing is not assisted by gravity. Moreover, cats and dogs do not typically drink water to assist swallowing. The purpose of the study reported here was to evaluate the esophageal passage of capsules in clinically normal cats and determine the incidence of entrapment and prolonged transit time.

Materials and Methods Animals—Twelve clinically normal adult cats were used for this study. Six (3 castrated males and 3 spayed females, between 2 and 10 years old) were client-owned animals; informed consent was obtained from the owners. Six (3 sexually intact males and 3 sexually intact females, between 1 and 4 years old) cats were owned by the University of Florida and maintained under conditions specified by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. These cats had not previously been used in any experimental study. None of the cats had a history or clinical signs of gastrointestinal tract disease. The 6 non–client-owned cats were observed for at least 1 week before the study. Fluoroscopy was used to determine that all cats had normal esophageal motility (ie, boluses of food and contrast were transported from the oropharynx to the stomach in < 15 seconds). Food was withheld for 12 hours, and then each cat voluntarily ate a small meal (1 to 2 ounces) of a commercial cat food a mixed with barium sulfate paste. The cats were fed while enclosed in a plastic pet carrier. The carrier was placed between the x-ray tube and image intensifier of the fluoroscope, which minimized stress and allowed cats to be observed without the need for manual restraint. The cats remained sitting or standing while in the carrier. The formation and transport of at least 4 boluses of food and contrast was observed fluoroscopically.

Experimental protocol—To simulate clinical conditions, cats were not habituated to the procedure or the radiography room. Food was withheld for 12 hours before the study, but cats were allowed free access to water. Number-4 capsules (5 X 14 mm) filled with barium sulfate powder were administered orally, and cats were immediately allowed to retreat into a plastic pet carriers that had been placed between the x-ray tube and image intensifier of the fluoroscope. Capsules were administered without lubrication. Fluoroscopy was performed through the pet carrier. The passage of the capsule was observed continuously for the first 60 seconds and then every 15 seconds. The study was terminated when the capsule reached the stomach. Transit time was recorded. If the capsule failed to reach the stomach and had remained fixed in place in the esophagus for at least 1 minute with at least 4 minutes having elapsed since administration of the capsule, then the study was terminated. A classification system does not exist for esophageal transit times in cats. We developed an arbitrary classification. # Esophageal transit of capsules in clinically normal cats

John P. Graham, MVB, MSc; Alan H. Lipman, DVM; Susan M. Newell, DVM, MS; Gregory D. Roberts, DVM, MS

Objective—To evaluate the esophageal passage of capsules in clinically normal cats and determine the incidence of prolonged transit or entrapment. Animals—12 clinically normal adult cats. Procedure—Esophageal transit of barium sulfatefilled capsules was evaluated fluoroscopically. Each cat was examined 3 times (36 examinations). Esophageal transit times were classified as normal (≤30 seconds) or prolonged (> 30 but ≤240 seconds). Capsules were considered entrapped when transit times were > 240 seconds. Results—Transit times were normal in 10 of the 36 (27.8%) examinations, whereas times were prolonged in 7 (19.4%) examinations. Capsules became entrapped in the midcervical region of the esophagus during 19 (52.8%) examinations. Following termination of each examination, cats with entrapped capsules were fed a small amount (0.5 to 1 ounce) of food; this resulted in passage of the capsule to the stomach. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance—The possibility of medication-induced esophagitis should be considered when orally administering ulcerogenic drugs to cats. It is recommended that a small volume of food be given following medications to ensure complete esophageal clearance. (Am J Vet Res 2000;61: 655–657)

Results Normal transit times were observed in 10 of 36 (27.8%) examinations. In 7 (19.4%) examinations, transit times were prolonged, whereas the capsule became entrapped during 19 (52.8%) examinations (Table 1). The capsule did not pass to the stomach during at least 1 examination in 9 of 12 cats. This occurred during all 3 examinations in 4 cats. Entrapped capsules were located in the midcervical region of the esophagus. Following termination of the study, cats with entrapped capsules were fed a small amount (0.5 to 1 ounce) of fooda; this resulted in passage of the capsule to the stomach.

Discussion The esophageal phase of swallowing consists of the transit of food boluses from the cranial portion of the esophagus to the gastro-esophageal junction.11,12 Primary and secondary peristaltic waves are normally present in the esophagus. Primary waves are a continuation of the pharyngeal peristaltic wave and pass smoothly down the esophagus in 5 to 8 seconds. There is a refractory period after a primary wave during which another primary wave cannot be initiated. If repeated swallowing efforts are made during this period, food will accumulate in the proximal portion of the esophagus. Secondary waves are stimulated by residual food left by a primary wave or by accumulation of food from repeated swallowing efforts during the refractory period. Impulses for a primary wave originate in the medulla, whereas secondary waves are initiated partly by intrinsic neural circuits in the esophageal myenteric nervous system and partly by reflexes transmitted by vagal afferent and efferent fibers to and from the medulla, respectively. A minimum quantity of material

must be present to stimulate a secondary wave. Swallowing of tablets or capsules is most likely accomplished by primary esophageal waves, as the volume of the medication is unlikely to be sufficient to stimulate a secondary wave unless water or food is swallowed after the medication. Prolonged esophageal passage or entrapment of capsules and tablets is a common phenomenon in humans. Esophageal passage of tablets was evaluated in 98 patients with gastrointestinal tract disease; prolonged transit times were detected in 57.1 Of these 57 patients, 21 had evidence of esophageal disease. Some of the patients with normal tablet transit times had esophageal abnormalities, such as hiatal hernia. In another study,3 entrapment of gelatin capsules occurred in the proximal portion of the esophagus in 39% of the healthy humans evaluated. This indicates that the problem of pill entrapment can be attributed only in part to preexisting subclinical or clinical esophageal disease. Results of another investigation2 indicated that failure of swallowing, classified as an esophageal transit time > 90 seconds, occurred during 22% of 726 swallowing examinations performed in humans, using a variety of tablets and capsules. Tablet entrapment occurred in 58% of 40 humans placed in a supine position immediately after ingesting barium tablets.13 Some investigators have detected a greater incidence of entrapment with capsules in comparison to tablets.2,4 This may be caused by the hygroscopic effects of gelatin capsules; capsules become tacky when moistened. Some tablets have similar properties or may be designed to swell to enhance dispersion of medication,6 which may result in prolonged contact or a greater concentration of the pharmaceutical at the site of entrapment. We used gelatin capsules filled with barium sulfate powder; mucosal adhesion may have been a factor in some examinations that revealed prolonged transit times or entrapment. Lubrication of the capsule would reduce the risk of mucosal adhesion and may be of benefit. The number-4 capsule is the smallest available size and is sometimes used when reformulating drugs for extra-label use. Commercial capsule formulations are not common. Clindamycin is available in capsule formation,b but the capsules used are larger than number 4. Although we evaluated esophageal transit of capsules only, entrapment of tablets has been detected in cats.10 Humans frequently drink with or after administration of tablets or capsules to facilitate swallowing. The incidence of entrapment was reduced but not eliminated in a group of healthy people by drinking 120 ml of water after swallowing capsules.3 Drinking 15 ml of water was found to improve transit of capsules when humans remained upright but had little effect when humans were in a supine position.13 The apparently greater incidence of entrapment when in a supine position and when tablets or capsules are swallowed without water has led to the recommendation that humans should remain upright and drink at least 15 ml of water after tablet administration.13 Moreover, suspensions rather than solid medications, especially capsules, should be used for bedridden patients.2 Domestic animals such as cats may be at increased risk of

esophageal pill or capsule entrapment, because water or food are not routinely given after medication, and the esophagus is oriented horizontally rather than vertically. Esophageal mucosal injury may develop by chemical or mechanical means. 14 Entrapment of tablets or capsules may result in chemical injury, because they disintegrate within the esophagus and result in prolonged exposure of esophageal mucosa to a high concentration of a given pharmaceutical. In humans, drugs such as emepromium bromide, steroidal and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, quinidine, potassium chloride, doxycycline, aspirin, alprenolol, propranolol, ferrosuccinate, and ferrosulfate have been shown to cause erosion and ulceration of esophageal mucosa. 5,6 Sustained release formulations may exacerbate these problems. 6 Doxycycline, oxytetracycline, alprenolol, propranolol, ferrosuccinate, ferrosulfate, and emepromium bromide have been reported to cause esophageal mucosal ulcers in cats. 15,16 The severity of esophageal injury is related to the depth at which the esophageal wall is affected (ie, involvement of the mucosa only or penetration to involve the submucosa and muscularis layers). 14 Injury to only the mucosal layer does not typically result in stricture formation, and clinical signs may be transient, mild, or nonspecific and, thus, may not attract the attention of the owner or lead to a definitive diagnosis. 14 Cats in the present study were determined to have normal esophageal function by observing the passage of multiple boluses of food and contrast material. We evaluated the ability of the esophagus to transport solids rather than liquids on the assumption that capsules and tablets would be handled as solids. All of the cats ate the meal voluntarily, eliminating the possible effects of force-feeding solids or liquids on pharyngeal and esophageal motility. Prolonged transit or entrapment was observed in all but 1 of the 12 cats during at least one examination; only 3 cats passed the capsule to the stomach in all 3 examinations. In 4 cats, capsules became entrapped during each examination. These results indicate there is individual variation among cats and some cats may be at greater risk of entrapment. The use of capsules rather than tablets may have contributed to the high incidence. Capsules were used rather than tablets, because they were easier to manufacture. Additional studies employing tablets are needed to determine what effect the formulation of a medication may have on esophageal transit in cats. Cats with entrapped capsules were given a small amount of food, and this resulted in complete clearance of the cap-

sule from the esophagus. We recommend that food be given routinely after oral administration of medications to cats unless specifically contraindicated. We did not investigate the effect of giving water after capsules became entrapped, but this could be considered an alternative to food. Elevating the head and neck may also be helpful, and lubrication of capsules may reduce the probability of mucosal adhesion.
